Hast
hast
v. (second person singular present of have; rendering Hebrew perfect forms with second-person subject, Greek echeis)
From Saxon hæfst, the second person singular present of habban. It follows thou as hath follows he. Like hath it serves both for possession and as the auxiliary forming the perfect tense.

Biblical Definition

Hast is thou hast — what one person possesses, or what one person has done. It carries the first question God ever asked about guilt: “Hast thou eaten of the tree, whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat?” (Genesis 3:11). The question is not for God's information but for Adam's confession, and the perfect tense makes evasion useless, since the deed is done and standing. The same form carries the sweetest acknowledgements in the Psalms: “For thou hast girded me with strength to battle” (2 Samuel 22:40), “Thou hast delivered me from the strivings of the people” (Psalm 18:43). It also carries the psalmist's hardest complaints, spoken to God rather than about Him: “But thou hast cast off and abhorred, thou hast been wroth with thine anointed” (Psalm 89:38). And it appears in the mouth of the wicked servant returning his master's money unused: “lo, there thou hast that is thine” (Matthew 25:25). Praise, protest, and self-justification all use the same verb, and all three are addressed to a Person who already knows the answer.

Webster 1828 Definition

The second person singular of the present tense of have; used only with thou. In Scripture it frames the first question of guilt in Eden, the psalmist's acknowledgements and complaints, and the excuse of the unprofitable servant.

expand to see more

HAST, v. [Sax. hæfst.] The second person singular of the present tense of have; as, thou hast.

2. To possess; to hold; as, thou hast riches.

3. As an auxiliary, it forms the perfect tense; as, thou hast spoken, thou hast done.

4. It is used only with thou; with ye or you the form is have.

5. In Scripture, Hast thou eaten of the tree? Gen. 3; thou hast delivered me from the strivings of the people, Psa. 18.

Key Scripture

Genesis 3:11 — "And he said, Who told thee that thou wast naked? Hast thou eaten of the tree, whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat?"

Psalm 18:43 — "Thou hast delivered me from the strivings of the people; and thou hast made me the head of the heathen: a people whom I have not known shall serve me."

Psalm 89:38 — "But thou hast cast off and abhorred, thou hast been wroth with thine anointed."

Matthew 25:25 — "And I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth: lo, there thou hast that is thine."

Modern Corruption

God's question in Eden is commonly read as though the Almighty were gathering information, which makes it either redundant or dishonest. It is neither: it is the summons to confession, and the whole biblical doctrine of repentance is contained in the form of it.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is confession as God's appointed means of dealing with known sin. The LORD does not ask Hast thou eaten because He is uncertain; He is omniscient, and the fig leaves had already answered Him. He asks because a sinner must say it himself. The pattern holds throughout Scripture: Cain is asked where his brother is, David is confronted by Nathan, Peter is asked three times whether he loves the Lord. In every case the question invites the words that repentance requires.

Adam's reply is the first evasion in human history and remains the model of all the others — The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat. The confession is technically complete and morally worthless, because it arrives at the truth only after routing the blame through the wife and, past her, through God Himself. The parable of the talents shows the same instinct dressed as piety: I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth: lo, there thou hast that is thine. Both men answer the question. Neither one repents.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew expresses thou hast by the second person perfect of the verb, or by yesh with a preposition for possession; Greek uses echeis and the second singular perfect; Saxon hæfst gives the English form.

expand to see more

Hebrew second person perfect — the completed act with thou as subject; the form of the LORD's question in Genesis 3:11.

Hebrew 'akal (H398) — to eat; the verb in the first question of guilt put to man.

Greek echeis (G2192) — thou hast; the second person singular present of echo.

Greek perfect tense — a completed act with abiding result; underlies most of the Authorized Version's thou hast.

Saxon hæfst — the Old English second singular present, retained with thou in the Authorized Version.

Usage

"Of the first summons to confession: Hast thou eaten of the tree, whereof I commanded thee? (Genesis 3:11)."

"Of deliverance acknowledged to God: Thou hast delivered me from the strivings of the people (Psalm 18:43)."

"Of the unprofitable servant returning what he never used: lo, there thou hast that is thine (Matthew 25:25)."
